name: Arabushi (unmolded katsuobushi)
text: Arabushi is katsuobushi dried to its target moisture without any mold (kabi) stage. It is the dark, smoke-scented form of the product and the base of most commercial shavings: items sold as katsuo kezuri-bushi or hana-katsuo are described as unmolded arabushi, and most supermarket shavings are arabushi. The traditional regional styles are named Yaizu, Satsuma, Tosa and Izu.
flavor: Strong smoky aroma and a forceful, direct katsuo taste; darker, blackish surface.
use: Dashi where power and smoke are wanted, and the usual stock for soba and udon shops, hot pots and everyday cooking; also the starting material that is later scraped and molded into karebushi.
craft: Judge by colour: blackish means no mold, brown means molded karebushi. Because tar and fat remain on the surface, arabushi gives a heavier, smokier stock than honkarebushi, so check the smoke note against the dish before choosing it.

name: Karebushi and honkarebushi (mold-cured katsuobushi)
text: Karebushi is made from arabushi by scraping off the tar and surface fat and then applying mold and drying at least twice. Honkarebushi repeats the mold-and-dry cycle further; sources give about 4 to 6 cycles as common, though there is no strict rule, and completion takes from 3 months to more than half a year. Ibusuki-Yamakawa in Kagoshima is cited as Japan's top producer of honkarebushi.
flavor: Mellow, refined, rounder aroma than arabushi; lighter smoke, deeper cured note.
use: Premium ichiban dashi and clear soups where clarity and elegance are required; shaved fresh at the counter in high-end kitchens.
craft: Brown, molded surface (not the black of arabushi) is the first visual cue. Ask the maker how many mold cycles were applied; the count is not standardised, so grade claims differ between makers.

name: Regional katsuobushi styles (Yaizu, Satsuma, Tosa, Izu)
ja: 焼津節・薩摩節・土佐節・伊豆節
text: Katsuobushi is traditionally classified by production region as Yaizu-bushi, Satsuma-bushi, Tosa-bushi and Izu-bushi. The source adds that Kochi, which gave Tosa-bushi its name, now produces mostly soda-bushi rather than katsuobushi. Details of how each style differs were not given in the sources consulted.
flavor: Regional character varies by maker; no standard comparison in the sources.
use: The regional name is used on packaging and by wholesalers to indicate the origin of the katsuobushi.
craft: Treat the regional label as origin information, not a grade. Compare by arabushi/karebushi type and shaving, since the sources give no standard that separates the four regional styles.
src: Koizumi Press - types of bushi and dashi

name: Soda-bushi (frigate mackerel bushi)
text: Soda-bushi is made from soda-gatsuo (frigate mackerel), centred on Tosashimizu in Kochi. It has a high proportion of blood meat, so the dashi is dense in flavour and aroma. Sources describe it as less suited to delicate refined cooking and as mainly used for soba dashi; soba shops often use soda for the dipping sauce of mori-soba.
flavor: Dense, heavy kokumi with a strong aroma and noticeable blood-meat richness.
use: Soba tsuyu, especially for cold mori-soba dipping sauce; blended with other fushi in commercial dashi; thick-shaved soda gives a stock with rich koku and aroma compared with thick-shaved katsuo.
craft: Because the flavour is strong, use it where it has to stand up to kaeshi (soy-sweet base); the usual shop practice cited is soda for mori, saba-bushi for kake soba.
src: Fushitaka - katsuo, maguro, soda and saba bushi

name: Saba-bushi (mackerel bushi)
text: Saba-bushi is dried and smoked mackerel processed in the style of katsuobushi. Sources describe a strong umami and little aroma, with sweetness and depth; they disagree on acidity, one saying there is no sourness and another a slight sourness.
flavor: Strong umami, sweet and deep, light aroma; possible faint acidity.
use: Broth for kake-soba and udon; often blended with uruime-bushi; soba shops commonly pair saba for kake and soda for mori.
craft: Because sources disagree on acidity, taste each lot rather than assuming; its low aroma makes it a good body-builder in mixed fushi.
src: Fushitaka - katsuo, maguro, soda and saba bushi

name: Uruime-bushi (round herring bushi)
text: Uruime-bushi is a bushi made from uruime-iwashi (round herring). It is described as having a rich kokumi and in the Kansai region is used for udon dashi; it is generally blended with saba-bushi rather than used alone.
flavor: Full-bodied, rich koku.
use: Udon dashi in Kansai; component of blended fushi.
craft: Blend ratio against saba-bushi is the maker's decision; the sources give no fixed proportion.

name: Maguro-bushi (tuna bushi)
text: Maguro-bushi is bushi made from tuna. The stock is pale and mild, described as suited to delicate clear soups (suimono); versions with the blood meat removed give an even lighter colour and a refined finish.
flavor: Light colour, mild, clean taste.
use: Clear soups and dishes where colour must stay pale.
craft: Choose blood-meat-removed (chiai-nuki) for the palest result; sources describe it as lighter than katsuo stocks.
src: Fushitaka - katsuo, maguro, soda and saba bushi

name: Kongo-bushi (blended fushi for professional dashi)
text: Kongo-bushi, also sold as gyomu dashi, is a blend of several shaved bushi, typically soda-bushi, saba-bushi and uruime-bushi. Professional shops use it because it has stronger umami than katsuobushi, a rounded sweetness and koku, and a lower price.
flavor: Heavy, sweet, kokumi-driven; less delicate than katsuo-only stock.
use: Noodle shop and casual restaurant dashi in volume.
craft: Check the label for which bushi are included and in what order; the blend determines whether it suits mori (soda-heavy) or kake (saba-heavy).

name: Hana-katsuo and kezuribushi labelling
text: On retail packs, products labelled katsuo kezuri-bushi or hana-katsuo are described as unmolded arabushi shavings, and most supermarket shavings are arabushi. A shaving labelled soda or katsuo atsu-kezuri (thick shaving) yields a stock with more body: soda atsu-kezuri gives rich koku and aroma, katsuo atsu-kezuri the characteristic katsuo aroma and umami.
flavor: Thin shavings give a quick, fragrant extraction; thick shavings give a richer, longer stock.
use: Choose thin shavings for quick finishing, thick for stock kettles.
craft: Read the species and the mold status on the label; the shaving thickness suits the dashi time.

name: Ibuki iriko (Ibukijima niboshi)
text: Iriko from Ibukijima in Kagawa Prefecture is made from katakuchi iwashi (Japanese anchovy). Each net-owner (amimoto) carries out the whole chain from catch through steaming to drying, and production runs from June to September. It is the regional specialty used for Sanuki udon dashi.
flavor: Clear, sweet iriko stock suited to udon.
use: Sanuki udon dashi; miso soup; any iriko stock.
craft: Because the catch, steam and dry are done by one house, ask the amimoto for freshness and harvest date; oxidised fat (abura-yake) is the main defect to check for.

name: Nagasaki niboshi
text: The Nagasaki Prefecture fisheries federation states that Nagasaki niboshi are cooked in seawater. Niboshi in general are mostly made from katakuchi iwashi; larger fish give a fuller dashi with more fat and koku, and smaller fish a lighter one.
flavor: Larger fish: rich koku; smaller: light.
use: Miso soup, noodle broths and general dashi; choose size by desired body.
craft: Seawater cooking is the origin-specific detail cited; for dashi, head and guts are the source of bitterness, so remove them when serving to customers.

name: Hirako-iwashi niboshi
text: Hirako-iwashi are small iwashi niboshi with small heads and guts. The source describes the dashi as free of bitterness and off-notes, with koku and a refined character, so they can be used whole.
flavor: Rich but clean, without bitterness.
use: Whole in mizudashi or simmered; refined miso soup and noodle broth.
craft: Their small viscera mean heads and guts matter less, but check each lot for oxidation.

name: Niboshi preparation: heads, guts, mizudashi
ja: 煮干しの下処理と水出し
text: Heads and guts of niboshi are the main source of bitterness and off-notes, so they are normally removed before making dashi; for dishes served to customers the advice is to prepare properly. Cold-water extraction (mizudashi) is said to give a cleaner stock. A quoted guideline is 25 to 30 g of niboshi per litre, about 5 fish per bowl of miso soup. Some say pretreatment is unnecessary in mizudashi because less scum comes out.
flavor: Cleaner, rounder stock from pre-treated fish; stronger and rougher from whole.
use: Niboshi dashi for miso soup, udon and ramen bases.
craft: Tear off heads, split and remove the black guts, optionally dry-roast; mizudashi in the fridge. Sources differ on whether pre-treatment is needed in cold extraction.

name: Donko and koshin (dried shiitake grades)
text: Donko (冬菇) are thick-fleshed dried shiitake whose caps are only 50 to 60 percent open, with a rounded cap and fine cracks on the surface. Koshin (香信) are thinner with fully opened caps and rehydrate faster.
flavor: Donko: meaty and concentrated; koshin: lighter.
use: Donko for simmered dishes and as a showpiece; koshin for dashi and quick preparations.
craft: Judge the cap thickness and the cracking pattern; note that rehydration time depends on the type.

name: Dried shiitake cold rehydration (5-5-10 rule)
text: Producer groups describe a 5-5-10 rule: 5 degrees C cold water, about 5 hours for thin koshin and 10 hours for thick donko. Cold water is said to preserve the enzyme activity that forms guanylic acid, while hot water or microwave rehydration is said to reduce umami. Another source recommends 24 hours in cold water for donko, so recommended times differ.
flavor: Cold-soaked liquor is rich in umami; the mushroom stays plump.
use: Shiitake dashi and simmered shiitake; keep the soaking liquid.
craft: Fridge, covered, fully submerged; start earlier for donko. Sources disagree on time (10 h vs 24 h), so test with your own product.

name: Kanpyo (dried gourd strips)
text: Kanpyo is yugao (bottle gourd) flesh peeled into ribbons and sun-dried. Tochigi accounts for nearly all of Japan's output: 209 t of a national 210 t in 2020, and 164 t, 99.4 percent, in FY2022 per the MAFF survey cited. National output has fallen from 447 t in 2000 to 258 t in 2018. The centre is Shimotsuke, Oyama and Mibu; one gourd of about 7 kg yields about 150 to 200 g. The main cultivar named is Kawachi-shiro.
flavor: Mild, sweet, slightly fibrous; takes up dashi and soy.
use: Binding and filling for makizushi and futomaki; ties for kombu-maki and fukuro dishes; simmered in dashi.
craft: Figures differ by year and source. Imported kanpyo is also on the market, though the claim that over 80 percent is Chinese was not verified.

name: Hotate hoshi-kaibashira (dried scallop adductor)
text: Dried scallop adductors from Hokkaido's Okhotsk coast are salt-boiled then dried. According to MAFF, larger pieces have richer umami while small pieces taste saltier. Saroma-ko scallops are noted for size; inner-lagoon scallops are said to be creamy-sweet and outer-sea ones crisp. The Hokkaido fisheries federation grades by individual weight: LL 12 g to under 16 g, L 8.6 g to under 12 g.
flavor: Concentrated sweet umami; firm, chewy.
use: Soaked and shredded into soups, rice dishes and XO-style sauces; the soaking liquid is kept as stock.
craft: Judge firm flesh, colour, gloss and fragrance; select size by saltiness and richness.

name: Tama-rei (frozen scallop adductor)
text: Tama-rei is the shucked scallop adductor frozen on its own, sold in size grades such as 2S and 3S; a 1 kg pack of 2S is about 36 to 40 pieces. It is the raw material from which dried adductors are made.
flavor: Sweet, clean raw scallop flavour.
use: Sashimi, sushi, grilling, and as raw material for kaibashira.
craft: Size code reflects count per kg; check thawed texture and drip.

name: Kuragakoi kombu (cellar-aged kombu)
text: Kuragakoi is a traditional Tsuruga method of ageing kombu in a storehouse. Okui Kaiseido revived it in 1989, applying it to Rishiri kombu from Fukahama in Rebun; they age for a minimum of 1 year and up to 2 to 3 years or more. The maker states that this removes the kombu and sea smell and increases umami. Aged lots can be kept even longer.
flavor: Rounder, less marine smell, more umami as claimed by the maker.
use: Kaiseki and high-end ichiban dashi.
craft: The time is the maker's claim; compare aged and fresh lots by taste.

name: Hine-mono and ohine (aged kombu terms)
text: One Hidaka kombu seller calls kombu aged one year hinemono (囲物), and aged two or more years ohine (大囲). This is a single seller's classification, not an official one.
flavor: Aged: mellower.
use: Reading kombu labels.
craft: Terms are seller-defined; always ask age.

name: Ittoken (first-grade inspection) kombu
text: Kombu quality is partly determined by the shore (hama) where it is harvested, with the best called betsukaku hama and graded first class. One retailer states that first-grade Rishiri kombu is about 1 m long, with shorter pieces graded second and third. This is a retailer description, not an official standard.
flavor: First grade: well-formed, long, clean blades.
use: Reading grade labels.
craft: Grade reflects shore and size; verify with supplier.

name: Tsuruga tesuki oboro kombu (hand-shaved)
ja: 敦賀の手すきおぼろ昆布
text: Hand-shaved oboro kombu is made by softening kombu in vinegar and shaving the surface by hand, one sheet at a time; mechanisation is difficult. Tsuruga's oboro process was registered as a national intangible folk cultural property in March 2025. Tsuruga kombu processing is said to date to the Horeki era in the 18th century. Tororo is machine-shaved from the sides of a compressed block of vinegared kombu.
flavor: Silky, delicate, dissolving; faint acidity from vinegar.
use: Wrapped around rice balls, floated in clear soup.
craft: Check thinness and whether it is hand-shaved (tesuki).

name: Shio-kombu (shiofuki kombu)
text: Shio-kombu is kombu simmered down in a soy-based liquid. One maker says a similar recipe existed in the Heian period, and the dry salt-bloomed kind (shiofuki kombu) came from wartime rationing, when drying was used to distinguish it from tsukudani. This is a single maker's account.
flavor: Salty-sweet, umami-dense.
use: Rice topping, pickling aid, seasoning.
craft: Salt bloom indicates dry shiofuki type.

name: Arame (Ise arame)
text: Arame is a brown seaweed of the kelp order with a branching blade. Mie Prefecture produces most of Japan's supply, about 200 t a year. It is wild only (not cultivated) and harvested July to September, then sun-dried to remove astringency, steamed, pressed, cut and dried. In Obama, Fukui it is simmered sweet for Buddhist observances.
flavor: Mild, soft, slightly sweet.
use: Simmered with aburaage and vegetables; shredded and dressed with soy.
craft: A soak of 5 to 10 minutes is the guideline; do not confuse with hijiki.

name: Kajime
text: Kajime is a kelp-order brown seaweed eaten in Okunoto, Ishikawa. It is mucilaginous. Sources conflict on edibility: one says only young astringency-free kajime is eaten while another says arame is edible and kajime is not, but local eating is documented. A guideline is to soak in fresh water about 2 hours if it tastes astringent.
flavor: Mucilaginous, slightly astringent.
use: Raw chopped with soy; soups.
craft: Taste raw first; soak if astringent.

name: Ichiban dashi, soba-shop method
text: A soba-oriented method published by Nisshin: bring kombu to 60 degrees C, hold on very low heat for 1 to 2 hours until sweet, remove it, heat to 80 degrees C (83 for frozen fushi) and add 15 to 20 g of shavings per litre without stirring. Home recipes elsewhere give 60 degrees C kombu extraction and say 70 degrees and above brings off-flavours.
flavor: Sweet kombu base with clean katsuo.
use: Kaeshi dilution for soba tsuyu.
craft: Do not stir the bushi, let it sink; do not exceed 80 degrees C.

name: Niban dashi (second dashi)
text: Niban dashi is made from the kombu and bushi left after ichiban dashi. Published methods differ: one heats to 70 to 80 degrees C and keeps it low for 3 to 4 hours; another boils then simmers about 10 minutes.
flavor: Lighter, rounder.
use: Simmered dishes and miso soup.
craft: Methods differ; settle on a time by tasting.
